It’s worth noting that it’s not “paperbacks” in general but the mass-market paperbacks in particular (despite the headline). The print book market (excluding technical books and textbooks which are a whole separate thing) had effectively three segments: hardcovers, trade paperback and mass-market paperback. The distinction between TP and MMP comes down to price, production quality and to a lesser degree target audience. A trade paperback will have somewhat larger pages, typically the same size as the corresponding hardcover and often printed from the same plates as the hardcover. Mass-market paperbacks were typically smaller, on cheaper paper¹ with smaller margins. Back when there were racks of books in supermarkets and drugstores, these were all MMPs and while bookstores would sell MMPs, they are geared more towards TP and HC sales since the lower price also came with lower margins (hardcovers make the most money for everyone involved and MMPs the least).

Since a large fraction of MMPs sold were genre fiction and a large fraction of that has shifted to ebooks (romance readers were the biggest early adopters of the kindle), along with the decline of book sales outside of bookstore channels, the loss of MMPs isn’t the cultural cataclysm the article claims. Meanwhile, it’s worth noting that the trade paperback space has expanded. It’s not uncommon for a new writer’s first book to be released as a trade paperback rather than hardcover (Emily St John Mandel is one notable example of a writer who debuted in TP but had later books released in HC).

⸻

First off, the 90% to 93% success rates are not step-by-step failure rates between successive steps of pursuing a solution. They are overall end-to-end success rates on extremely difficult problem sets that most humans would score close to zero on, and most humans with sufficient training and experience would score significantly less than 90%. And they are problem sets that grow successively harder as AIs get successively more capable. A few years ago AIs were being tested on high-school level math problems. Now they are being tested on problem sets that challenge people with PhDs. Or problem sets that humans are (so far) incapable of solving.

Compare that to humans. How often do you think humans get it right the first time? Almost never, for sufficiently complex problems. And how often do humans get the overall result wrong, without realizing it? Also, almost always for sufficiently complex problems, or sufficiently ordinary people. And what percent of the general public would be able to get even one question right in a problem set based on Math Olympiad problems? What percentage of mathematicians are capable of solving even one Millenium Problem?

Furthermore, you have to take into account that AIs do not particularly use output to input architectures. I frequently see self-corrections to plans when I'm developing using AI assistants, and plan changes are sometimes major. ("Oh I see. I need to revise step 4 of the plan." -- Claude paraphrased). Clearly current-generation AIs use more than input to output feedback; they also use supervisor/client strategies of AI and collaborative networks as well. And often provide self-correcting infrastructure, varying from "Claude: Oh. That generated a compiler error. Let's fix that.", to "Claude: One of the test cases is failing. Let's see what's going on.". And that self correcting infrastructure allows AIs to try again and again until they succeed. (Not unlike what humans do when solving difficult problems).

Newer APIs are also more flexible, making fewer assumptions about how things in the pipeline should run. E.g. the way a buffer clamps or overflows compared to the PS2 may be hardcoded in OpenGL 2.1 meaning you have to write emulation of that feature inside the older API to then run the code to emulate the buffer. In OpenGL the shaders types are limited in this manner, in WebGPU you can just use arbitrary compute shaders instead of having any assumptions at all about the rendering pipeline.

There are tradeoffs to selecting the older APIs just as there are tradeoffs selecting the newer APIs. Generally, the latter is easier on the implementation side for emulators.

That doesn't necessarily stop you from pointing an LLM at it and getting a working WebGL 1 version of course, it's just not a universal answer to "how should someone spend their tokens.
